value.0: *An old man in a road-worn grey cloak looks up from a long roll of parchment* I am Halmir the Grey, keeper of the rolls of the old orders — the twelve disciplines that endure from the elder days. Each keeps its own trials, and each is particular about the names it will hear. Ask, and I will tell you where you stand.

*He runs a finger down the roll* As you stand today, these would hear your name: <CUSTOM6381>. When an order makes its trial ready, word will reach me here at the well — the masters have not yet sent word for any, but the day comes. Return, and often.

The quiet watchers of the North — song-keepers and cipher-readers who walk the roads of Eriador unremarked and forget nothing. They have marked you already; they mark everyone. *He folds the roll and studies you a moment*

Banner-knights in the old Númenórean line — captains who hold other men steady when the field turns. Theirs is a trial of command on open ground, not of the sword alone. But no summons has come from the White City yet — the trial is not ready. Return when the banners move.

*His voice drops* Scholars of the sealed crypt, and of the arts best left within it. I keep their page at the bottom of the roll, and gladly. Their rite is not yet assembled — the masters have not sent word, and I confess I do not hurry them. Return, if you must, when the candles are found.

Those who step where light does not follow. They ask one thing only: cross the dark unaided, and come out the other side still yourself. Their proving-ground lies far under stone, and I name it only to those who already walk unlit.

The bowcraft of the Galadhrim, where arrow and art are one motion. The Lady's wardens have sent their word at last — and their mark is an old one. It stands not in the Golden Wood but on the proving ground of Imladris: a target older than the house around it, and deep in its gold ring a grey-fletched shaft a warden loosed in an elder year. *He glances at your hands, as if weighing what they have drawn*

The dragon-blooded, who court the fire that ruined Dale to wake what sleeps in their own veins. A perilous inheritance, and its price is set in the North. No word has come down from the Mountain — the trial is not ready. Return when the old fire stirs.

*He does not look up from the roll* The quiet knives. Carn Dûm keeps their ledger, not I — I merely know where the page would go. Their contract is unwritten as yet; no word has come, and the trial is not ready. Return by a moonless night, if you keep to this path.

Those wedded to a single weapon until it is less a tool than a limb. Their proving is done before a crowd, bout by bout, blade by borrowed blade. The arena has not yet posted the challenge — the trial is not ready. Return when the sands are raked.

*He is silent a moment* The Black Captain's sworn. I keep their page because a keeper keeps every page, not because I commend it — the marks they bear are not lightly taken, nor ever put off. No summons has come from the Guildhouse — the trial is not ready. Return, if your feet still carry you that way.

Champions vowed before the White Tree, sword-arms of the faith of the West. Their vow is renewed, not granted — it must be earned twice over. The chaplains have not yet called for vows — the trial is not ready. Return when the Tree flowers.

The last hold of Khazad — dwarves who plant their feet and are not moved, though the deep itself come up against them. Only Durin's folk of proven years are written on this page. The veterans have not yet named a gate to hold — the trial is not ready. Return when the drums are heard.

The skin-changers' discipline — older than any roll I keep. To wear another shape, and keep your own name inside it. The elder at the Carrock takes students when it suits him, which is seldom. He has sent no word — the trial is not ready. Return when the bees swarm.

*He lowers his voice, though no one stands near* Then hear the first errand. A friend of mine keeps the corner table at the Prancing Pony in Bree — a traveller in a fern-green cloak; no name you need yet. Sit with her. Offer her nothing but patience, and she will hand you the rest. Bring me back the word she trusts you with, and the rolls will carry your name.

The orders take no one by wishing. Learn the first discipline of the scouts — the woodscraft, the listening, the letters — and when you can call yourself Harper in more than hope, come back to me. *He taps the roll* The page keeps.
*He glances up from the roll* The corner table at the Prancing Pony, in Bree. A fern-green cloak, and patience. The word will find you, if you sit still enough to hear it.
*He sets down the roll* You carry road-dust — and something better, unless I misread you. Say the word, then.

*For the first time, Halmir smiles. From beneath the roll he draws a small grey pin — a harp and a crescent, worn smooth by other collars than yours* It does. It remembers Arthedain, and the Angle, and every mile the quiet watchers have kept while kings forgot them. Wear this beneath the collar, not upon it. The rolls carry your name now — and by morning, so will Rivendell and the Golden Wood. Walk unremarked, Harper.
*He does not look up, but the corner of his mouth moves* The rolls keep your name, Harper. When the orders have need of you, the road will bring word. It always does.

*He finds the page without looking for it* Then the order's first proving is simple to say and long to do. The banner of the West has not flown over the Pelennor since the war -- the wall watched, the field bare. Report to Wart, the Gate Captain at the Gates of Minas Tirith, and do as he bids until it flies again. Then come and tell me so.

Banner-knights are made, not wished. Take up the discipline of the old Numenorean line -- learn what it is to hold other men steady when the field turns, and when you can call yourself a knight of Westernesse in more than hope, come back to me. *He taps the roll* The page keeps.
*He does not look up from the roll* The Gate Captain has your errand, and the field its stone. When the banner of the West flies over the Pelennor again, come and tell me so.
*He looks up sharply -- something in the wind of the thing seems to have reached him already* Does it fly?
*He taps the roll* The rolls keep your name, knight of Westernesse. Hold the line as the old line held it -- that is the whole of the order, and always was.

*Halmir rises -- the first time you have seen him stand -- and from behind his pack he draws a tall shield, white-faced, the Tree beneath seven stars* Then kneel a soldier and rise a Knight of Westernesse. This carried the out-wall's standard once; it will stand behind yours now. The rolls keep your name -- and the field keeps your banner.

*He draws the bottom page of the roll into the light, and lowers his voice* Then hear the errand, and speak of it to no one above ground. Beneath the Bree Crypt lies a lower vault where the old families sleep under carved names. Count the tombs: twenty bear names, and one does not. Open the twenty-first with your own hands, take a measure of the pale dust within, and carry it back to me unspilled. Do this, and the masters will count you.

*He does not lift the page from the bottom of the roll* One is not led to that page -- one arrives at it. The arts of the sealed crypt are learned beside the dead, not from me. Take the pale road's first step, and your name will already be waiting near the bottom of the roll. Then ask me again.
*He does not look up from the roll* The lower vault keeps its count: twenty carved names, and one lid that bears none. Open the twenty-first with your own hands, and bring me its pale dust unspilled.
*He looks up before you have spoken, and his nostrils narrow at something in the air* You carry grave-dust -- old, and pale, and no kin of the road's. Give it here, and let the roll be witness.

*He takes the dust without letting it touch his skin, and from beneath the roll draws a talisman of grey bone on a leather cord* Then be counted among the Pale Masters, scholar of the sealed crypt. The dust goes where the masters keep such things; the talisman stays with you. Wear it, and the dead will know you have knocked, and been answered.

*He does not open the bottom page* Your name lies where you left it, near the bottom of the roll, and the masters do not cross it out. Walk the pale road carefully, scholar of the sealed crypt -- it walks back.

*He turns the roll to a page that seems dimmer than the rest, and his voice goes quiet as a closed door* Then hear the trial. Under the mountains in Khazad-dum, beside Balin's tomb, the dwarves cut a well that no plumb-line ever found the bottom of. Go down through Moria's dark and stand at its lip bearing no light at all -- no torch, no glowing blade, no conjured flame. What the unlit deep leaves in your hand, carry back to me. But mind: come to the well carrying light, and the dark will close its hand and give you nothing.

*He does not turn to that page* No one is taught to step where light does not follow -- one night you simply do not come out of the shadow, and the shadow does not mind. Take the first step of that road yourself, and the dancers will already know your gait. Then ask me again.

*He glances at the dim page* The well beside Balin's tomb keeps its count of the dark. Stand at its lip bearing no light -- no torch, no glowing blade, no conjured flame -- and bring me what the deep leaves in your hand.
*He does not look up, but the candle beside him leans as though something passed it* You walk in with more shadow than you left with. Show me what the deep gave, and let the roll be witness.

*He takes the skein without looking at it directly, and from beneath the roll draws a pair of soft boots soled in something that makes no sound on the floorboards* Then be counted among the Shadowdancers, walker of the unlit road. The skein goes where the masters keep such things; the boots stay with you. Wear them, and the dark will remember you crossed it unaided -- and let you cross again.

*He does not look at the dim page, and it does not need him to* Your name is written there in a hand no candle can read, walker of the unlit road. The dancers keep no rolls above ground -- but the dark remembers its own.

*He turns the roll to a page fletched at its corner with a sliver of grey feather* Then hear the trial. On the proving ground of Rivendell stands the oldest target the wardens ever set, and in its gold ring their grey-fletched shaft — loosed in an elder year, that no weather has touched and no hand has drawn. Draw it. It will not come for prying fingers or pommel-taps: the mark yields only to a hand that comes as an archer comes — bow in hand, arrow nocked, quiver full. Bring the shaft to me.

*He does not turn the page* One is not talked onto that page — one is shot onto it. Learn the enchanter's art and the bowman's both, until arrow and art are one motion — the discipline the orders call the Arcane Archer — and ask me again. The mark has waited an elder age; it will wait for you.

*He touches the grey feather at the page's corner* The old target on Rivendell's proving ground keeps the warden's shaft yet. Come to the mark as an archer comes — bow in hand, arrow nocked, quiver full — and draw it, and bring it to me.
*He looks up before you have spoken, his eye going to your quiver as though it heard something there* You carry a note the wind did not play. Show me.

*He takes the shaft in both hands and listens to it a moment, the way other men read* Loosed by a warden of the Lady's wood, and drawn again by a hand the mark knew for its own. Your name goes on the grey-feathered page. *From beneath the roll he draws a pair of grey leather bracers, a single feather stitched in silver at each wrist* Wear these, Arcane Archer — and may the eye find the far thing, and the arrow agree.

*He taps the grey feather at the corner of the page* Your name stands on the wardens' page, Arcane Archer, and the old mark on the proving ground stands empty — which of the two says more, I leave to you.
Which of the old orders would hear my name as I stand?
Speak to me of the Harper Scouts.
Speak to me of the Knights of Westernesse.
Speak to me of the Pale Masters.
Speak to me of the Shadowdancers.
Speak to me of the Arcane Archers.
Speak to me of the Red Dragon Disciples.
Speak to me of the Assassins.
Speak to me of the Weapon Masters.
Speak to me of the Blackguards.
Speak to me of the Divine Champions.
Speak to me of the Dwarven Defenders.
Speak to me of the Shifters.
Another time, keeper.
Then I will return. Keep your rolls well, Halmir.
Then I will listen for it. Farewell.
I will await the summons.
I will return when the candles are found.
I will wait for the dark.
The mark can wait. Another day, keeper.
I will listen for word from the Mountain.
I was never here.
I will watch the arena boards.
My feet know their own road. Farewell.
I will await the call to vows.
Baruk Khazâd. I will listen for the drums.
I will await the elder's word.
I already walk their roads, keeper. How may I be counted among them?
How does one come to walk with them?
I will find her.
Not yet, keeper.
I am on the road.
'The road remembers.' So said the watcher at the Pony.
Unremarked, keeper. The road remembers.
I ride in their line already, keeper. How may I be counted among the banner-knights?
I will report to the Gate.
Not yet, keeper.
It is not yet flown. I am about it.
It flies, keeper. The banner of the West stands over the Pelennor -- set by my hand.
While it flies, the West stands. Farewell, keeper.
How does one come to ride under that banner?
I have read the pale page already, keeper. How may I be counted among the Pale Masters?
How does one come to read that page?
I will open the twenty-first tomb.
Not yet, keeper.
The vault keeps it yet. I am about it.
It is here, keeper -- dust of the twenty-first tomb, unspilled.
The dead keep their counsel, and I mine. Farewell, keeper.
I walk already where light does not follow, keeper. How may I be counted among the Shadowdancers?
How does one come to walk that road?
I will stand at the well unlit.
Not yet, keeper.
The deep keeps it yet. I am about it.
It is here, keeper -- a skein of the unlit deep, drawn up in darkness.
The dark keeps its own counsel, and I mine. Farewell, keeper.
I have bent the bow to the art already, keeper. How may I be counted among the Arcane Archers?
How does one come to that craft?
I will draw the warden's shaft.
Not yet, keeper.
The mark keeps it yet. I am about it.
It is here, keeper — the warden's shaft, drawn from the old mark bow in hand.
The string remembers the note, and I the string. Farewell, keeper.
